Key Research Thinking Patterns: Common-Garden Experimental Dissection: Isolating genetic versus environmental contributions to phenotypic variation by rearing wild-caught or hybrid lineages in controlled factorial designs (e.g., factorial 2x2 common-garden experimental design for Poecilia mexicana cave and surface ecotypes).

Behavioral Assay Standardization: Quantifying complex social and cognitive traits through rigorous, repeatable observational protocols to establish welfare standards and evolutionary baselines (e.g., standardized binary choice social preference tests and spatial learning assays).

Geographic and Ecotypic Comparison: Evaluating local adaptation and sexual selection dynamics by contrasting sympatric and allopatric populations across distinct environmental gradients (e.g., geographic comparison of mate choice preferences in Limia perugiae across salinity regimes in Hispaniola).

Hybrid Speciation Pathway Analysis: Tracing the breakdown of reproductive isolation and the transition to asexuality by analyzing postzygotic barriers and fitness costs in unisexual lineages (e.g., reciprocal F1 hybrid crossing experiments and population sampling from sympatric zones of Poecilia formosa).

Cognitive-Behavioral Syndrome Integration: Linking mating system pressures to cognitive evolution by assessing how coercive versus mixed male tactics shape female cognitive flexibility and boldness (e.g., multivariate analysis of cognitive-behavioral syndromes in Xiphophorus nigrensis and Gambusia vittata).
Summary Description: Ingo Schlupp is an evolutionary biologist specializing in the behavioral ecology and comparative cognition of livebearing fishes. His research integrates hybrid speciation mechanisms with rigorous welfare assessments, primarily utilizing the Amazon molly (Poecilia formosa) and Poecilia mexicana systems. He investigates the evolutionary transition from sexuality to asexuality and the maintenance of reproductive isolation through common-garden experiments and reciprocal hybrid crosses. Expanding into sexual selection, Schlupp employs dichotomous choice tests to evaluate male mate choice and local adaptation across geographic gradients. Recently, he has incorporated comparative cognition, using mesocosm-reared populations to assess how mating tactics shape female cognitive-behavioral syndromes. His work bridges fundamental evolutionary theory with applied animal welfare, establishing refined husbandry protocols and understanding the ecological drivers of behavioral diversity.
